public_rationale: The 2025 evidence supports reported coding utility alongside recurrent material errors. In Stack Overflow's 2025 survey, approximately 70% of agent users reported time savings on development tasks; these were perceived benefits, not measured gains [e1]. In news responses generated in late May and early June 2025, the EBU/BBC evaluation found significant issues in 45% of responses across four assistants [e2]. Its comparable BBC subset improved from 51% to 37%, showing progress alongside persistent problems [e2]. METR's experiment using February–June 2025 tools found that experienced developers took 19% longer on familiar repositories despite believing AI saved time, limiting broader claims of coding productivity gains [e3].
limitations: Coding utility is supported here by self-reports; the experiment does not establish gains across coding tasks [e1, e3].
The multi-assistant reliability evaluation concerns news responses, not every ordinary application [e2].
These 2025 findings do not establish that unreliability is unavoidable in all applications or future systems [e1, e2, e3].

our_interpretation: The ordinary reading is that useful applications coexist with recurrent, material errors that make unchecked reliance unsafe. It does not mean every output is wrong.
I use 2025, the latest complete calendar year before the post, as the reporting period for this ongoing state.
I assess systems then available. A claim that no future generative system could become reliable would require different evidence.

criteria.contradiction_condition: Representative evaluations show dependable performance across ordinary uses without material verification needs, or credible evidence defeats the assertion that any practical coding uses exist.

evidence.locator: AI → AI Agents, Impacts of AI agents
evidence.explanation: Developer respondents report useful applications in their work, supporting the modest assertion that practical coding uses exist. Self-selection and subjective productivity estimates limit the strength of this evidence.

Responses generated in late May and early June across four assistants and multiple languages contained significant problems in 45% of cases. The report also records improvement in the comparable BBC subset, so persistent problems do not imply no progress.

In this experiment, experienced developers working on familiar repositories became slower despite believing AI helped. This limits reliance on perceived productivity and broad claims of coding gains, but does not negate the existence of some useful applications.
